question: How can efficient approximate inference and learning be done in directed probabilistic models with continuous latent variables that have intractable posteriors, on large datasets?
hypothesis: A reparameterised variational lower bound can be optimised with standard stochastic gradients, and a learned recognition model gives faster convergence and better bounds than wake-sleep and Monte Carlo EM.
contributions: A reparameterization of the variational lower bound gives a lower bound estimator (SGVB) optimisable with standard stochastic gradient methods.
For i.i.d. datasets with per-datapoint continuous latents, fit an approximate inference (recognition) model to the intractable posterior using SGVB (AEVB).

method.summary: Trains a VAE: a one-hidden-layer MLP encoder gives a diagonal Gaussian q(z|x), a one-hidden-layer MLP decoder gives Bernoulli or Gaussian p(x|z), with prior N(0,I). Encoder and decoder are trained jointly by Adagrad on the SGVB lower bound with the reparameterization trick, and compared with wake-sleep and Monte Carlo EM on MNIST and Frey Face.
method.task: generative modelling of images with continuous latent variables (variational lower bound and marginal likelihood)

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.split: Ntrain = 1000 and 50000 in the marginal-likelihood comparison; the full set is used in the lower-bound comparison (size not stated)

datasets.name: Frey Face
datasets.preprocessing: continuous data, so Gaussian decoder with means constrained to (0,1) by a sigmoid

models.name: AEVB / VAE
models.architecture: MLP encoder and MLP decoder, each with a single hidden layer, tanh; Gaussian diagonal q(z|x); Bernoulli (MNIST) or Gaussian (Frey Face) decoder

models.name: Monte Carlo EM (HMC)
models.architecture: no encoder; samples latents with Hybrid Monte Carlo

training.objective: SGVB lower bound (eq. 7/10) plus small weight decay equal to prior p(theta)=N(0,I); approximate MAP
training.lr: Adagrad global stepsize chosen from {0.01, 0.02, 0.1} by training-set performance in the first few iterations
training.lr_schedule: Adagrad with accompanying annealing schedule (stated for the MCEM comparison)
training.weight_decay: small, corresponding to p(theta)=N(0,I); value not stated
training.hardware: Intel Xeon CPU at an effective 40 GFLOPS

other.MCEM: 10 HMC leapfrog steps with stepsize tuned for 90% acceptance, then 5 weight update steps

inference.samples: marginal likelihood estimated on the first 1000 datapoints of train and test sets, 50 posterior samples each via HMC with 4 leapfrog steps

metrics.name: variational lower bound per datapoint
metrics.definition: estimated average lower bound per datapoint

metrics.name: estimated marginal log-likelihood
metrics.definition: MCMC-based estimator of appendix D, 3 latent dims

eval.protocol: Train and test curves vs number of training samples evaluated; single runs, no seeds or significance tests stated; estimator variance said small (<1) and omitted.

availability.data: MNIST and Frey Face (link in footnote)

evidence.quote: Minibatches of size M = 100 were used, with L = 1 samples per datapoint.

results.claim: AEVB converged considerably faster and reached a better lower bound than wake-sleep in all experiments, for every latent dimensionality.
results.setup: MNIST (Nz 3-200) and Frey Face (Nz 2-20), one-hidden-layer MLPs, Adagrad, M=100, L=1
results.note: Read from curves in Fig 2; no numeric values in text.

results.claim: More latent variables did not cause more overfitting, attributed to the regularizing effect of the bound.
results.setup: MNIST Nz up to 200, lower bound on train and test

results.claim: One sample per datapoint suffices when the minibatch is large enough.
results.quote: we found that the number of samples L per datapoint can be set to 1 as long as the minibatch size M was large enough, e.g. M = 100

results.claim: The lower-bound estimator variance was small.
results.setup: Fig 2 average lower bound per datapoint
results.quote: The estimator variance was small (< 1) and omitted.

results.setup: Intel Xeon CPU at effective 40 GFLOPS
results.quote: Computation took around 20-40 minutes per million training samples with a Intel Xeon CPU running at an effective 40 GFLOPS.

results.claim: AEVB converged faster than wake-sleep and MCEM on estimated marginal likelihood, for small and large training sets; MCEM cannot be applied efficiently to full MNIST.
results.setup: MNIST, Ntrain 1000 and 50000, 3 latent variables, 100 hidden units
results.note: Read from Fig 3; the text only says results are in Fig 3 and that MCEM is not on-line.

results.claim: The marginal likelihood estimator is only reliable for latent spaces under 5 dimensions.
results.quote: as long as the dimensionality of the sampled space is low (less then 5 dimensions)

limits: No numeric results in the text; all comparisons are curves in Fig 2 and Fig 3.
Only MNIST and Frey Face, shallow MLPs; hierarchical/convolutional models, time series and full VB on parameters are left to future work.
Marginal likelihood comparison limited to 3 latent dimensions because estimates get unreliable above that.
Posterior assumed diagonal Gaussian (stated as a choice, not a limitation of the method); only continuous latents.
Hidden-unit counts chosen from prior autoencoder literature; no seeds or repeated runs reported.
Dataset sizes, step counts and weight decay value not stated.

terms.definition: an approximation q_phi(z|x) to the intractable true posterior, also called a probabilistic encoder
p_theta(x|z): given a code z it produces a distribution over the possible corresponding values of x
Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes: a reparameterized differentiable unbiased estimator of the variational lower bound
Auto-Encoding VB: SGVB used to optimise a recognition model for i.i.d. data with per-datapoint continuous latents
AEVB with a neural network as the recognition model

code.snippet: L(theta,phi;x) ~ 1/2 sum_j (1 + log(sigma_j^2) - mu_j^2 - sigma_j^2) + 1/L sum_l log p_theta(x|z^(l)), z^(l) = mu + sigma * eps^(l), eps ~ N(0,I)
